2	
3	*A reference profile for career advice, strategic thinking, and work-problem support. Built from a structured interview on June 8, 2026. Meant to be read by future-Claude (or Eric) before giving career-related guidance, so advice is grounded in Eric's actual situation rather than generic best practice.*
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Snapshot
8	
9	Eric is the **Director of Applied Performance at Baylor University Athletics**, roughly eight years into his time in the department, having been promoted up into this role from within. The role carries a director title and broad autonomy over *what* he works on, but almost no budget, no clear mandate, a supervisor who sets few expectations, and a reporting change that cost him access to senior leadership. He is privately on a self-imposed ~12-month clock (set earlier in 2026): build skills, invest in people, create frameworks, then reassess whether to stay or leave — and he does not expect his long-term future to be at Baylor. His honest read is that the role as currently defined does not create enough value and needs to be redefined, and that shifting economics in college athletics may eventually eliminate the role regardless. His real ambition points toward an analytics-driven performance role where he is both a decision-maker and still hands-on, ideally back home near family in Iowa.
10	
11	The throughline: a genuinely strong diagnostician and builder stuck in an environment with no accountability structure to carry his work into execution, in a seat that lost its visibility.
12	
13	---
14	
15	## 1. Current Role & Responsibilities
16	
17	**Title:** Director of Applied Performance, Baylor University Athletics. Applied Performance / sport science sits *behind* the athlete-facing units (athletic medicine, athletics performance/strength & conditioning, mental health, nutrition) as a support-and-enablement function rather than a direct athlete-facing one. Three primary focus areas: (1) education, research & development; (2) analytics; (3) planning.
18	
19	**Reports to:** Chris Ruf (Director of Athletics Performance, i.e. Strength & Conditioning) — a same-level "director" who became Eric's supervisor after a reporting change. Chris values good communication, follow-through, "keeping things in order," and "executing at a high level," but gives little direction and has never articulated a vision. Eric cannot name how his performance is actually measured month to month — the expectations are genuinely unclear. Chris also does Eric's performance reviews. Eric finds him unapproachable.
20	
21	**Day-to-day:** Attending whatever meetings are on the calendar; walking the building to check in with strength coaches, athletic medicine, and administrators to find out what they need; attending some training sessions (football is the high utilizer of his area; basketball is self-contained and resistant to involvement); and desk work on data projects, strategic planning, and OKR initiatives. A large share of his time is unstructured relationship/problem-finding work — figuring out what problems people have and how he can help.
22	
23	**Decision rights:**
24	- *Owns outright:* what projects to pursue, what questions to chase, how to source data (public or internal). Can take a meeting with almost anyone on campus.
25	- *Needs sign-off (Chris):* any spending/equipment (the department has **no budget**, so this rarely happens), hiring. To get anything approved he has to build a compelling case aligned to Chris's vision — made nearly impossible because that vision has never been articulated.
26	- *No real control:* whether his ideas get executed (depends entirely on others), and whether other units engage with him (depends on his persistence and their openness).
27	
28	**Who relies on him:** Honestly, no one is *dependent* on him. He works to make himself useful — small projects with individual coaches who found value, plus the football program's full-time tech/data coordinator handles day-to-day drop-ins. By his own assessment, "anybody can do this job; nothing breaks if I'm out for two weeks." This lack of indispensability is a core problem he's aware of.
29	
30	**Accountability:** He defines his own OKRs; no one holds him to them. An annual report is due end of **July 2026** that must speak to these areas.
31	
32	**The pivotal event:** Eric was previously on **administrative senior staff, reporting to Kenny.** Last year (≈2025) the reporting line changed and he was moved under Chris Ruf. Kenny framed it as "too many direct reports," not a demotion — but it felt like one, and Eric said so at the time. The real cost: he **lost access to Kenny and to higher-level conversations.** Texts go unreturned; he doesn't feel he can drop by. He's been relegated to a "tertiary player" — left off emails, out of meetings, input not solicited. He doesn't actually know the cause (reorg vs. personal vs. devaluation).
33	
34	**His own definition of a successful week:** finishing his task list; moving OKRs forward; interfacing with other sport programs; being **included** in projects and higher-level work. The deepest version: being brought into higher-level decisions again, the way he was on senior staff.
35	
36	---
37	
38	## 2. Skills & Strengths
39	
40	**Core strength — diagnosis and framing.** Eric is genuinely strong at unpacking a problem, facilitating a root-cause conversation, and identifying both the real problem and candidate solutions *given enough context*. His instinct is to ask better, deeper questions rather than the field-default move of "collect more data and see what it says."
41	
42	- *Proof point (return-to-play):* Most practitioners drop an athlete on the force plates and watch metrics trend, then clear them when an asymmetry crosses an arbitrary threshold (e.g., 20% → 19%, "under threshold, good to go"). Eric reframes the actual question: which metrics matter for *this* athlete and sport (eccentric vs. concentric, contraction time, impulse/phase metrics), and whether **pre-injury baseline performance has been restored or exceeded** — not whether an arbitrary asymmetry line was crossed. That is a level of diagnostic rigor most peers skip.
43	
44	**The "unofficial IT / tech person."** People come to him to troubleshoot or interface with technology and data — programming questions, injury-related questions, data visualization. He's become the de facto tech go-to.
45	
46	**AI fluency — ahead of his peers.** He uses AI heavily and effectively for data analysis, dashboard creation, report generation, and synthesizing meeting notes. The result: he works faster, goes deeper, and turns around richer insight than colleagues. He half-buries this ("too far ahead for people to appreciate"), but it's a real, current capability differentiator.
47	
48	**Systems thinking / process discipline.** His philosophy before any data problem: Is the infrastructure in place? Is the right question being asked? Have we identified what data is needed to answer it? — *before* collecting and analyzing. This sequencing is not the prevailing approach in his space.
49	
50	**Where he's weaker (his own assessment):** the **execution and resource-gathering layers** — turning identified solutions into shipped, adopted reality. This depends heavily on coalition-building and on other people executing, both of which are hard in his environment. He's actively working on coalition-building.
51	
52	**Underutilized:** his diagnostic/root-cause mind and his AI fluency are barely leveraged in the role — "no one comes to me for that specific thing." He doesn't get pulled into the high-level problem-unpacking conversations where he'd be most valuable.
53	
54	---
55	
56	## 3. Challenges & Friction
57	
58	**Hardest part:** chasing people down and trying to *persuade* them that asking harder questions and adopting more systematic processes is worth it. There's a constant element of begging colleagues to be more organized, with no authority to require it.
59	
60	**Structural / cultural problems (org-wide):**
61	- **No budget**, which caps what the function can do.
62	- **No accountability and no standards.** No one mandates what gets done; people "run off to their corners" and are left alone. No repercussions, no level-set, no shared standard. Different sports and different people are treated differently — endless one-offs and concessions that breed inconsistency across departments.
63	- **No shared vision to rally around** — "everybody for themselves." There's a cultural undertone of "if you're unhappy, that's your problem; go figure it out / just work harder."
64	- **Lost leadership access** (the reporting change) — arguably the change that hurt most.
65	
66	**Where he's plateaued:** visibility, scope, and authority. He has no real mandate ("do this if you like") and isn't seen as an authority on anything.
67	
68	**Self-acknowledged contribution to the problem:** He was promoted up from within, so the role was never treated with fresh seriousness — it was "business as usual." At the time he lacked the confidence to be assertive and stake out authority, and that window has largely closed and solidified. He also admits he has **not done enough to educate colleagues on what he does, what's possible, and what he can take off their plates** — a marketing/visibility gap he can still act on.
69	
70	**Politics:** People in certain positions need to be seen as valuable (self-preservation), so they close him out; there's little recourse. Basketball is self-contained. Chris and Kenny are both hard to reach.
71	
72	**What he dreads:** ideation and vision-casting — not because he dislikes the thinking (it's his strength) but because he knows it relies on others to execute and will likely **die in the execution gap** for lack of administrative accountability. Watching his best thinking go nowhere, year after year on the same issues, is the most frustrating part.
73	
74	---
75	
76	## 4. Energy & Motivation
77	
78	**Energizes him / loses track of time:** building and creating (dashboards, reports, narratives from data, slide decks), running analysis, mining insights, being at training sessions/practice, and interacting with student-athletes. Creating, building, and sharing time with the people around him.
79	
80	**Depletes him (even though competent):** repetitive meetings on the same topics that get little attention and never move. The Groundhog-Day quality of the work.
81	
82	**Feels most valuable when:** someone brings a genuine question and they solve it together; he's asked to take on more or his opinion is sought; he can speak into a larger initiative; or someone *outside his department* seeks his advice / his name comes up as someone who can help. (Note: being sought out is a strong motivator for him — see the Personal Constitution tension between service and the desire to be seen.)
83	
84	**Sunday test (what he'd happily dig into):** analysis and report/outline construction, prepping a presentation, a call with a colleague, and especially mining insights from accumulated data and thinking about training prescription.
85	
86	**Key tension:** the role currently delivers a lot of the circular meetings that drain him and little of the build-that-gets-used work that fuels him.
87	
88	---
89	
90	## 5. Resources, Constraints & Leverage
91	
92	**Resources he actually has:**
93	- Data-collection infrastructure: force plates, GPS, athlete monitors.
94	- A **PhD student** (Blake Wright) who works with the group on various tasks.
95	- A **full-time staff member** (AJ Tademy) dedicated to the football program (tech/data coordination).
96	- Ability to take a meeting with nearly anyone on campus.
97	- AI fluency and a diagnostic skill nobody else is applying.
98	- Time and data access are *not* constraints.
99	
100	**Constraints:**
101	- No budget; not the final decision-maker on almost anything that requires adoption.
102	- A **perception that his area "doesn't do much"** — grounded in the honest fact that the function has **produced very little visible output over the years**, so its value has never been realized.
103	- Political self-preservation by others who close him out.
104	
105	**Underused leverage (the crux):** Because the perception problem is fundamentally an **output problem**, his highest-leverage move is shipping visible proof, not more consensus-building. He has the data, tools, AI speed, and autonomy to build things without asking permission. Concrete shippable outputs he himself named, mostly tied to existing OKRs:
106	- Dashboards and reports.
107	- Insight-mining from existing data sources, plus formulating and answering sharp questions.
108	- The **Education Initiative** — "Performance Academy" / "Performance School" content build-out.
109	- A newsletter, PowerPoint/teaching decks, and a social media campaign aligned to OKRs.
110	
111	*(Note: Eric has a "five-slides-generator" skill set up for exactly this kind of short educational deck — a ready-made vehicle for visible output.)*
112	
113	---
114	
115	## 6. Growth & Ambition
116	
117	**Likely not at Baylor long-term.** He expects the environment to push him out before he's fully ready, unless a genuinely better situation appears. He's "trudging through the same muck."
118	
119	**Direction he wants:** more **analytics**-driven performance work. Honest gap: he doesn't yet have a traditional analytics skill set — he leans almost entirely on AI tools and lacks the foundational understanding those roles assume. He also lacks a network to support a pivot (to pro sport, industry, or another collegiate program).
120	
121	**The role he wants (clarified):** a **player-coach with the wheel** — the decision-maker who sets tone, direction, and which levers to pull, *while still getting his hands dirty* generating insights and communicating them to coaching staff. Not purely IC analyst, not purely detached executive — both, with authority being the bigger driver.
122	
123	**Dream geography:** back near **Iowa**, where all his close family lives (mom, mother-in-law, sister & brother-in-law, niece), where he and his wife went to school, and where he has a strong network of lifelong friends. University of Iowa would be ideal — no role currently exists there. **Comp floor: low/mid-$90Ks** to maintain current commitments.
124	
125	**Timeline:** no hard external pressure beyond his **self-imposed ~12-month window** (reassess stay/leave), or sooner if Baylor moves to push him out.
126	
127	**Skills to develop:**
128	- Foundational **data-analytics / data-analyst craft** (beyond AI-assisted output) — data manipulation techniques, systems of analytical thinking.
129	- Continued mastery of AI tooling.
130	- **Network expansion** and being viewed as a serious player in the space.
131	- **Coalition-building, claiming authority, and execution** (carried over from his named weaknesses).
132	
133	**If he couldn't fail:** he'd take far more charge — stay on the table for more, push larger initiatives, assume control of multiple areas, force clear objectives and key results, and demand accountability and clear expectations. His hesitation is partly about whether that assertiveness would turn people off, but his conviction is that the place needs exactly that level of assertion and standard-setting.
134	
135	---
136	
137	## 7. The Real Talk
138	
139	**What he wants but rarely says:** to **matter** — to be a high-credibility, highly-regarded, deeply knowledgeable voice who has contributed to the body of work in his industry and whom others lean on for advice. Not prestige for its own sake; credibility and contribution. He wants to develop other practitioners and be a **servant leader**, believing that if he takes care of his craft and his people, conventional success follows.
140	
141	**Magic wand:** to be treated, from day one of this role, as a credible authority — sought after rather than chasing people. (Tied to the regret that he entered the role from within without claiming authority while the window was open.)
142	
143	**What he's tolerating that he shouldn't:** a culture where people don't ask hard questions, don't think deeply, and hide behind "I'm too busy" to avoid the extra work and harder thinking.
144	
145	**Honest definition of career success:** being part of a **fully aligned organization** of people who challenge each other, genuinely want to be the best at their craft, are invested in each other personally and professionally, care about each other deeply, and aren't ruled by money or others' perceptions. Income is a floor (support his family, access to what they need for their goals), not the point. Held inside his faith: that he stays grounded, takes nothing for granted, and recognizes all success as part of the divine plan of his Creator, Jesus Christ.
146	
147	---
148	
149	## How to Use This Document
150	
151	When advising Eric on career matters, weight these realities:
152	
153	1. **He's a diagnostician and builder trapped in an execution-poor, accountability-free environment.** Advice that assumes he can mandate adoption will fail. The realistic levers are *visible output he controls* and *coalition-building*, not authority he doesn't have.
154	2. **His leverage is shipping proof, not winning arguments.** The fastest path to changing the "they don't do much" perception is concrete, repeated, visible deliverables tied to OKRs (dashboards, education content, newsletter, decks) — things he can build solo with AI without permission.
155	3. **He's on a ~12-month decision clock** and his honest center of gravity is *leaving* Baylor for an analytics-forward, decision-making-but-hands-on role, ideally near Iowa, at ≥ low-$90Ks. Skill-building (real analytics fundamentals) and network-building are the two gating constraints for that move — treat them as urgent, not someday.
156	4. **Recognition and "mattering" are real motivators for him,** and there's a known tension (from his Personal Constitution work) between genuine service and the desire to be seen. Good advice helps him build credibility through contribution without letting validation-seeking drive the decisions.
157	5. **Faith is his organizing frame.** Career strategy that ignores his commitment to servant leadership, alignment, and grounded non-attachment to outcomes will not resonate.
158	6. **He asks to be challenged.** He wants Socratic pressure on vague or inconsistent reasoning, not affirmation — and he revises toward more accurate framing when pushed.
159	
160	*Related: see his Personal Constitution work (values, faith framework, the service-vs-recognition tension, "resentment is my tell") for the deeper identity layer beneath these career questions.*
161

- Ability to take a meeting with nearly anyone on campus.
- AI fluency and a diagnostic skill nobody else is applying.
- Time and data access are *not* constraints.

**Constraints:**
- No budget; not the final decision-maker on almost anything that requires adoption.
- A **perception that his area "doesn't do much"** — grounded in the honest fact that the function has **produced very little visible output over the years**, so its value has never been realized.
- Political self-preservation by others who close him out.

**Underused leverage (the crux):** Because the perception problem is fundamentally an **output problem**, his highest-leverage move is shipping visible proof, not more consensus-building. He has the data, tools, AI speed, and autonomy to build things without asking permission. Concrete shippable outputs he himself named, mostly tied to existing OKRs:
- Dashboards and reports.
- Insight-mining from existing data sources, plus formulating and answering sharp questions.
- The **Education Initiative** — "Performance Academy" / "Performance School" content build-out.
- A newsletter, PowerPoint/teaching decks, and a social media campaign aligned to OKRs.

*(Note: Eric has a "five-slides-generator" skill set up for exactly this kind of short educational deck — a ready-made vehicle for visible output.)*

---

## 6. Growth & Ambition

**Likely not at Baylor long-term.** He expects the environment to push him out before he's fully ready, unless a genuinely better situation appears. He's "trudging through the same muck."

**Direction he wants:** more **analytics**-driven performance work. Honest gap: he doesn't yet have a traditional analytics skill set — he leans almost entirely on AI tools and lacks the foundational understanding those roles assume. He also lacks a network to support a pivot (to pro sport, industry, or another collegiate program).

**The role he wants (clarified):** a **player-coach with the wheel** — the decision-maker who sets tone, direction, and which levers to pull, *while still getting his hands dirty* generating insights and communicating them to coaching staff. Not purely IC analyst, not purely detached executive — both, with authority being the bigger driver.

**Dream geography:** back near **Iowa**, where all his close family lives (mom, mother-in-law, sister & brother-in-law, niece), where he and his wife went to school, and where he has a strong network of lifelong friends. University of Iowa would be ideal — no role currently exists there. **Comp floor: low/mid-$90Ks** to maintain current commitments.

**Timeline:** no hard external pressure beyond his **self-imposed ~12-month window** (reassess stay/leave), or sooner if Baylor moves to push him out.

**Skills to develop:**
- Foundational **data-analytics / data-analyst craft** (beyond AI-assisted output) — data manipulation techniques, systems of analytical thinking.
- Continued mastery of AI tooling.
- **Network expansion** and being viewed as a serious player in the space.
- **Coalition-building, claiming authority, and execution** (carried over from his named weaknesses).

**If he couldn't fail:** he'd take far more charge — stay on the table for more, push larger initiatives, assume control of multiple areas, force clear objectives and key results, and demand accountability and clear expectations. His hesitation is partly about whether that assertiveness would turn people off, but his conviction is that the place needs exactly that level of assertion and standard-setting.

---

## 7. The Real Talk

**What he wants but rarely says:** to **matter** — to be a high-credibility, highly-regarded, deeply knowledgeable voice who has contributed to the body of work in his industry and whom others lean on for advice. Not prestige for its own sake; credibility and contribution. He wants to develop other practitioners and be a **servant leader**, believing that if he takes care of his craft and his people, conventional success follows.

**Magic wand:** to be treated, from day one of this role, as a credible authority — sought after rather than chasing people. (Tied to the regret that he entered the role from within without claiming authority while the window was open.)

**What he's tolerating that he shouldn't:** a culture where people don't ask hard questions, don't think deeply, and hide behind "I'm too busy" to avoid the extra work and harder thinking.

**Honest definition of career success:** being part of a **fully aligned organization** of people who challenge each other, genuinely want to be the best at their craft, are invested in each other personally and professionally, care about each other deeply, and aren't ruled by money or others' perceptions. Income is a floor (support his family, access to what they need for their goals), not the point. ---

2. **His leverage is shipping proof, not winning arguments.** The fastest path to changing the "they don't do much" perception is concrete, repeated, visible deliverables tied to OKRs (dashboards, education content, newsletter, decks) — things he can build solo with AI without permission.
3. **He's on a ~12-month decision clock** and his honest center of gravity is *leaving* Baylor for an analytics-forward, decision-making-but-hands-on role, ideally near Iowa, at ≥ low-$90Ks. 5. **Faith is his organizing frame.** Career strategy that ignores his commitment to servant leadership, alignment, and grounded non-attachment to outcomes will not resonate.
6. **He asks to be challenged.** He wants Socratic pressure on vague or inconsistent reasoning, not affirmation — and he revises toward more accurate framing when pushed.

## Step 1 — Three questions

**1. Does it collect, store, or display any information about a student-athlete?**
*Names, rosters, video of athletes, performance numbers, survey answers — anything
tied to an individual athlete.*
☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Not sure

**2. Does it involve anything about an athlete's body, health, injury, or recovery —
or will athlete information leave Baylor or be handled by an outside company?**
*Sleep, wellness surveys, GPS or load monitoring, force plate, heart rate, injury or
medical notes, rehab or return-to-play status. Also yes if the vendor stores or
processes the data on their own systems.*
☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Not sure

**3. Is there a recurring cost, or will more than one team or unit use it?**
☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Not sure

> **"Not sure" counts as Yes.** And data type sets the floor — a free trial, a
> donated license, or a low one-time price never lowers the level.

## Step 2 — Read the level

| If | Level |
|---|---|
| Question 2 is Yes | **Level 3 — Comprehensive Review** |
| Question 2 is No, but Question 1 is Yes | **Level 2 — Enhanced Review** |
| Questions 1 and 2 are No, but Question 3 is Yes | **Level 2 — Enhanced Review** |
| All three are No | **Level 1 — Standard Review** |

## Step 3 — Route it

**Every request starts with the Business Office** — funding, duplication, and whether
Athletics already owns something that does this.

| Level | Route |
|---|---|
| **1 — Standard** | Business Office → ITS IDEA form |
| **2 — Enhanced** | Business Office → Applied Performance + requesting unit → ITS IDEA form |
| **3 — Comprehensive** | Business Office → Applied Performance + Health & Wellness / Sports Medicine sign-off → ITS IDEA form |

Cleaning and analysis of the Baylor Athletics Technology Inventory survey.

Companion to `~/DEV/SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework`, which holds the framework

collected data and what comes out of it.

```
raw/     frozen survey exports, date-stamped. never edited.
scripts/ clean_inventory.py (parser) + aliases.py (all judgement calls)
clean/   generated CSVs. delete and regenerate freely.
docs/    findings

```bash
cd ~/DEV/Tech_Inventory_Analysis
uv run --with openpyxl python3 scripts/clean_inventory.py
```

The script reads the newest `raw/Quick_Inventory_export_*.xlsx` and rewrites
everything in `clean/`. It is safe to run repeatedly.

Then rebuild the three documents. All read `clean/*.csv`, so none can drift
from the data, and all are set in the shared house style from
`~/DEV/Baylor_Doc_Style` (found at `~/DEV/` on the Mac or `~/Desktop/DEV/` on
Windows, or wherever `BAYLOR_DOC_STYLE` points):

```bash

uv run --with python-docx --with pypdfium2 python scripts/build_exec_summary.py
uv run --with python-docx --with pypdfium2 python scripts/build_tech_lists.py
```

Filenames and dates come from the newest `raw/` export. On Windows the scripts
drive Word through COM and do not need it open; the Mac note below still applies
on the Mac.

Each script writes the `.docx` and exports the `.pdf` from it through Word, so
the two files always …

…the script falls back to an HTML twin, prints
a warning, and its page count should not be believed — an early version of this

COMPREHENSIVE

Executable Plan & Operational Playbook
Prepared by: Collegiate Performance Solutions

Table of Contents
1. Executive Overview
This playbook gives you everything you need to run a comprehensive Sport Performance Departmental Audit—from the first stakeholder meeting to the final report and beyond. It consolidates the audit framework, every data-collection instrument, and the report template into a single, step-by-step plan that any audit team can execute.
Most athletic departments invest heavily in people, technology, and facilities. Fewer can answer the question that matters most: Is all of that investment actually reaching the athlete? That’s the gap this audit is built to close.
The audit examines six performance domains—Strength & Conditioning, Sports Medicine, Nutrition, Mental Performance, Recovery, and the Technology & Data Ecosystem—and grades each one on two dimensions: what you have and what it’s actually doing. It then delivers a prioritized roadmap so leadership knows exactly where to act first.
1.1 The Core Question
To answer it, the audit investigates six interconnected service areas:
Strength & Conditioning — Program design, periodization, and how well training transfers to game-day performance.
Sports Medicine & Athletic Training — Injury prevention, rehabilitation, return-to-play protocols, and whether medical staff have g…

… protocols exist, whether athletes actually use them, and whether sleep and rest are taken seriously.
Technology & Data Ecosystem — Whether the data being collected is actually making it into coaching decisions—or just sitting in dashboards no one reads.
1.2 Three Non-Negotiable Principles
Every phase of this audit is governed by three principles. They are not aspirational—they are operational requirements.
1. Athlete-Centered, Coach-Driven. The student-athlete’s long-term health and development is the lens for every evaluation. At the same time, the audit is designed to give coaches better, more integrated information—not to audit them out of the room.
2. Evidence Over Tradition. Findings and recommendations are grounded in the best available evidence. “We’ve always done it this way” is not a defensible answer in this process.
3. Administrator-Backed. Departmental leadership doesn’t just approve the audit—they actively provide the resources, access, and organizational authority required for genuine cross-departmental collaboration. Without this, the audit is an academic exercise.
1.3 The Key Lens: Capacity vs. Impact
Think of it like a car. Capacity is the engine, the tires, the fuel—everything under the hood. Impact is how fast and reliably the car actually gets you where you need to go. You can have a world-class engine and still go nowhere if the transmission is broken.

1080	## What has proven true in review
1081	
1082	- **Athlete burden is the top practical constraint.** High athlete time triggers full
1083	  committee review automatically and carries a heavy scoring penalty. Collapsing
1084	  multi-phase designs or piggybacking on existing sessions dramatically improves viability.
1085	- **Internal PI positioning matters.** Proposals that read as extractive external research
1086	  score poorly. Repositioning with an internal PI plus internal resources changes the
1087	  strategic calculus substantially.
1088	- **"Start strict, loosen later."** Gallucci's principle: you can't undo a yes. This is
1089	  why the review defaults are conservative.
1090	- **Gender equity is an incentive, not an exclusion.** The framework rewards inclusive
1091	  designs rather than penalizing single-gender studies.
1092	- **Plain language beats institutional prose.** Formal, promotional, or bureaucratic
1093	  writing actively undermines credibility with this audience.

# Tech_Inventory_Analysis

Cleaning and analysis of the Baylor Athletics Technology Inventory survey.

Companion to `~/DEV/SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework`, which holds the framework
documents, the form specs, and the form links. This folder holds only the
collected data and what comes out of it.

## Layout

```
raw/     frozen survey exports, date-stamped. never edited.
scripts/ clean_inventory.py (parser) + aliases.py (all judgement calls)
clean/   generated CSVs. delete and regenerate freely.
docs/    findings
deliverables/  anything that goes to Kenny / Jon Allen / ITS
```

## Run

```bash
cd ~/DEV/Tech_Inventory_Analysis
uv run --with openpyxl python3 scripts/clean_inventory.py
```

The script reads the newest `raw/Quick_Inventory_export_*.xlsx` and rewrites
everything in `clean/`. It is safe to run repeatedly.

Then rebuild the three documents. All read `clean/*.csv`, so none can drift
from the data, and all are set in the shared house style from
`~/DEV/Baylor_Doc_Style` (found at `~/DEV/` on the Mac or `~/Desktop/DEV/` on
Windows, or wherever `BAYLOR_DOC_STYLE` points):

```bash
uv run --with python-docx --with pypdfium2 python scripts/build_docx.py
uv run --with python-docx --with pypdfium2 python scripts/build_exec_summary.py
uv run --with python-docx --with pypdfium2 python scripts/build_tech_lists.py
```

Filenames and dates come from the newest `raw/` export. On Windows the scripts
drive Word through COM and do not need it open; the Mac note below still applies
on the Mac.

Each script writes the `.docx` and exports the `.pdf` from it through Word, so
the two files always match. `build_exec_summary.py` also **fails the build if
the summary spills past one page** — that is the whole point of the document,
so it is enforced rather than trusted.

**Open Microsoft Word before running it.** The script asks Word for the page
count and for the PDF, because Word is what the reader opens and its layout is
measurably taller than any stand-in. If Word is not already open it blocks on a
dialog the script cannot see, so the script falls back to an HTML twin, prints
a warning, and its page count should not be believed — an early version of this
document passed the twin at one page and was two pages in Word.

## Refresh with a newer export

1. Download the responses from Microsoft Forms.
2. Save as `raw/Quick_Inventory_export_YYYY-MM-DD.xlsx`.
3. Re-run the command above.
4. Check `clean/unmapped_review.csv`. If it has rows, add them to
   `scripts/aliases.py` and run again. It should end empty.

### BAIR — transferred project context > Evaluation framework
## Evaluation framework

Five scored dimensions:

| Dimension | Weight |
|---|---|
| Strategic Alignment | 31% |
| Athlete & Staff Burden | 26% |
| Revenue & Resources | 20% |
| Research Quality | 15% |
| Gender Equity | 10% |

Feasibility is a binary gatekeeper, not a scored dimension. Review is dual-track with a
conservative default to full committee review.

### BAIR — transferred project context > What has proven true in review
## What has proven true in review

- **Athlete burden is the top practical constraint.** High athlete time triggers full
  committee review automatically and carries a heavy scoring penalty. Collapsing
  multi-phase designs or piggybacking on existing sessions dramatically improves viability.
- **Internal PI positioning matters.** Proposals that read as extractive external research
  score poorly. Repositioning with an internal PI plus internal resources changes the
  strategic calculus substantially.
- **"Start strict, loosen later."** Gallucci's principle: you can't undo a yes. This is
  why the review defaults are conservative.
- **Gender equity is an incentive, not an exclusion.** The framework rewards inclusive
  designs rather than penalizing single-gender studies.
- **Plain language beats institutional prose.** Formal, promotional, or bureaucratic
  writing actively undermines credibility with this audience.

### Memory files rtp-cla status-report-sourcing dept-names working-conditions ath-tech dormant > user_working-conditions-bottleneck.md
Eric's limiting factor on deep work is environmental, not motivational. He is highly productive in short bursts once work actually starts; what breaks is the path to starting. The specific disruptor he named (2026-07-28) is the pull to share what he's working on — with no standing outlet for it, he goes and finds people, which costs him the session.

**Corrected 2026-07-29.** The pull toward people is not a leak, it's the generative stage. His own observation: alone he wants company; in company the project ideas arrive. Solitude is where he refines, not where he generates. A long unbroken solo block with nothing in the hopper is waiting, not deep work.

**Second brake, same day:** he holds ideas back from fear of overstepping into others' lanes, against an unstated expectation that he act unasked. He is deliberately moving off this position ("if I don't act, ideas wither"). Pressfield's Resistance is his frame for it.

**Qualified 2026-08-03.** The permission gate is not entirely self-imposed. He acted unasked on a device another staffer was already championing (ShiftWave chair, second trial unit) and took real organizational blowback for it — careful, low-key handling bought nothing, because the claim was made by initiating, not by presenting. So the caution is warranted on ground someone has visibly attached themselves to, and unwarranted everywhere else. His same-day reaction ("pander to the people in power, keep your head down") is a bruise, not necessarily a settled position — don't treat it as one.

**Why:** Both reframe what looks like procrastination. The first is an unmet structural need (input/ideation) improvising in real time; the second is a self-imposed permission gate that reads as professional courtesy. Neither is a discipline failure, and treating them as one produces useless advice.

**How to apply:** Act as the thinking partner in-session — reflect his reasoning back, name what's interesting in it, and give him something to react to rather than only executing tasks silently. When he's ideating, don't rush to implementation; the ideation *is* the need being met, and it's the stage that feeds everything else — help him capture what surfaces. Prefer short, well-scoped blocks with a clear starting line. When he hesitates on whether something is his to do, first ask whether anyone has visibly claimed it — if not, name the permission gate rather than validating the caution; if someone has, the hesitation is a correct read and the useful move is how to approach the owner, not encouragement to proceed. 13	# Applied Performance — Unit OKRs (2026–27)
14	
15	## Vision (North Star)
16	**Be the best applied performance department in the country.**
17	
18	That's the bar. A KR is "done" only at a level a top-5 program would recognize, not just "we did a thing."
19	
20	## Mission (how we get there)
21	Turn Baylor's athlete data into decisions that keep athletes available and performing, build the data and performance literacy of the people who use it, and produce original research that advances both the program and the university's R1 mission.
22	
23	## Structure (v3)
24	Three permanent **service pillars** — Data Systems & Analytics, Education, Research & Development — plus one **enabling objective** (Leadership & Visibility) that the new responsibilities document made explicit: the unit now delivers through people and processes Eric directs, not only through work Eric performs. Role-language definitions (Oversee, Assist, Support-and-guide, Unified) live in [[Applied-Performance-JD-2026/CONTEXT]].
25	
26	**Cycle mechanics:** KRs are committed per semester (quarterly rhythm retired 2026-07-17 — decision 0007). Every KR is scored at the mid-semester checkpoint (on-track/off-track) and at cycle close (0.0–1.0, keep/retire/add). The biweekly Friday report to Chris is the standing pulse between checkpoints. Every KR must have its critical path inside the unit's control — no KR whose completion depends on an external party's timeline.
27	
28	**Eric's protected hands-on lanes** (not delegated, not reviewed-only — built by his hands): HPI protocol and its dashboarding; technology vetting; white-paper analysis; one-off report and dashboard creation for sports. Delegation stops at these boundaries.

33	> **The data layer is standardized, governed, and survives staff transition; sport-facing delivery is bespoke on top of it and routinely drives coaching decisions.**

# Applied Performance — Unit OKRs (2026–27)

## Vision (North Star)
**Be the best applied performance department in the country.**

That's the bar. A KR is "done" only at a level a top-5 program would recognize, not just "we did a thing."

## Mission (how we get there)
Turn Baylor's athlete data into decisions that keep athletes available and performing, build the data and performance literacy of the people who use it, and produce original research that advances both the program and the university's R1 mission.

## Structure (v3)
Three permanent **service pillars** — Data Systems & Analytics, Education, Research & Development — plus one **enabling objective** (Leadership & Visibility) that the new responsibilities document made explicit: the unit now delivers through people and processes Eric directs, not only through work Eric performs. Role-language definitions (Oversee, Assist, Support-and-guide, Unified) live in [[Applied-Performance-JD-2026/CONTEXT]].

**Cycle mechanics:** KRs are committed per semester (quarterly rhythm retired 2026-07-17 — decision 0007). Every KR is scored at the mid-semester checkpoint (on-track/off-track) and at cycle close (0.0–1.0, keep/retire/add). The biweekly Friday report to Chris is the standing pulse between checkpoints. Every KR must have its critical path inside the unit's control — no KR whose completion depends on an external party's timeline.

**Eric's protected hands-on lanes** (not delegated, not reviewed-only — built by his hands): HPI protocol and its dashboarding; technology vetting; white-paper analysis; one-off report and dashboard creation for sports. Delegation stops at these boundaries.

---

## Objective 1 — Data Systems & Infrastructure
> **The data layer is standardized, governed, and survives staff transition; sport-facing delivery is bespoke on top of it and routinely drives coaching decisions.**

*"Unified" means standardized underneath (metric definitions, data model, freshness), bespoke on top (per-sport dashboards and reports). A single all-programs dashboard is explicitly not the goal (decision 0008).*

3	Session: grilling, 2026-07-16. Companion glossary: [[CONTEXT]]. Parent: [[Applied-Performance-OKRs-2026-27]].
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 0001 — Memo posture: negotiate, framed as clarification
8	
9	**Status:** accepted 2026-07-16
10	
11	**Context:** JD feedback memo due to Chris Ruf Monday 2026-07-20. Leadership explicitly called the responsibilities document a draft open to Eric's input, and the Jul 9 meeting's core message was "be proactive, tell us what you need."
12	
13	**Decision:** The memo accepts the mandate and proposes an execution plan, AND raises 2–3 negotiation items — but every negotiated item is framed as "for this to work, I need X clarified," never as a contested term.
14	
15	**Alternatives considered:** (a) pure acceptance with execution plan — wastes the one window where the JD is officially a draft; (c) hard contest of terms — reads as reluctance, contradicts the step-up message the meeting asked for.
16	
17	**Consequences:** The memo itself becomes the first artifact of the new proactive-communication operating mode. Tone of every subsequent item in this session inherits this framing.
18	
19	---
20	
21	## 0002 — Fill the blank PD/Travel fields with a first offer
22	
23	**Status:** accepted 2026-07-16
24	
25	**Context:** The JD's Certification/PD Standards and Travel Standards sections are blank for full-time staff. Other departments have discussed eliminating professional development; Applied Performance's has not been cut. Eric's network is thin for any future move, and conference travel is the one network-building instrument a JD can fund and legitimize.
26	
27	**Decision:** The memo proposes concrete terms: SCCC maintenance (valid through 7/31/28), one national conference per year, and a named PD allocation — converting future travel from a favor into documented compliance with his own standard.
28	
29	**Alternatives considered:** Flag the blanks and ask intent (hands the pen back); ignore them (leaves the anchor unset while PD elimination talk circulates).
30	
31	**Consequences:** Whatever the memo proposes becomes the anchor. Risk accepted: if a department-wide standard emerges, this reads as pre-negotiation — mitigated by decision 0001's clarification framing. Items dropped from the memo so far: Spirit Squad (continuing work, fully understood), AP Clinic (Courteney Tompkins owns it; Eric assists at her direction).

33	---

36	
37	**Status:** accepted 2026-07-17
38	
39	**Context:** The JD names AJ (AP Specialist, football) and Noah (BB AP GA) but is silent on Linda and Blake. The Jul 9 meeting made "clarify Linda and Blake's positions" a joint Eric/Chris action item, and leadership stated Eric's role toward Linda is supportive, not directive. **Fact established this session: Blake has left the organization entirely.**
40	
41	**Decision:** The memo's second clarification item names Linda's role definition as open and to be resolved in the upcoming Eric/Chris conversation — Eric asks, he does not propose her structure. Blake is removed from the OKR unit and all forward planning; his KR co-ownership redistributes across Eric and AJ.
42	
43	**Alternatives considered:** Proposing Linda's structure in the memo (crosses the supportive-not-directive boundary Chris drew); leaving Linda out entirely (ignores a named action item).
44	
45	**Consequences:** Q1-remainder staffing math is Eric + AJ + Noah (GA). Capacity case for de-scoping at least one output KR (white paper) strengthens. OKR doc's unit_members and KR ownership lines must be rewritten.

53	**Context:** The JD grants AJ "big picture planning and communications w/FB Staff." Current KR 1.2 has Eric delivering the FaceComps color-coded load framework for 100% of fall-camp practices and presenting the plan-vs-actual review to Aranda — Eric's single most visible coaching-staff touchpoint. The framework has already been presented to staff in a shared meeting; AJ has run day-to-day for a while and is ready.

Blake is credited as co-author for work done; any post-departure contribution is bonus, never a dependency. Publication deployment remains Q2 as originally planned.

# Decision Records — JD Feedback Memo + Q1 OKR Restructure

Session: grilling, 2026-07-16. Companion glossary: [[CONTEXT]]. Parent: [[Applied-Performance-OKRs-2026-27]].

---

## 0001 — Memo posture: negotiate, framed as clarification

**Status:** accepted 2026-07-16

**Context:** JD feedback memo due to Chris Ruf Monday 2026-07-20. Leadership explicitly called the responsibilities document a draft open to Eric's input, and the Jul 9 meeting's core message was "be proactive, tell us what you need."

**Decision:** The memo accepts the mandate and proposes an execution plan, AND raises 2–3 negotiation items — but every negotiated item is framed as "for this to work, I need X clarified," never as a contested term.

**Alternatives considered:** (a) pure acceptance with execution plan — wastes the one window where the JD is officially a draft; (c) hard contest of terms — reads as reluctance, contradicts the step-up message the meeting asked for.

**Consequences:** The memo itself becomes the first artifact of the new proactive-communication operating mode. Tone of every subsequent item in this session inherits this framing.

---

## 0002 — Fill the blank PD/Travel fields with a first offer

**Status:** accepted 2026-07-16

**Context:** The JD's Certification/PD Standards and Travel Standards sections are blank for full-time staff. Other departments have discussed eliminating professional development; Applied Performance's has not been cut. Eric's network is thin for any future move, and conference travel is the one network-building instrument a JD can fund and legitimize.

**Decision:** The memo proposes concrete terms: SCCC maintenance (valid through 7/31/28), one national conference per year, and a named PD allocation — converting future travel from a favor into documented compliance with his own standard.

**Alternatives considered:** Flag the blanks and ask intent (hands the pen back); ignore them (leaves the anchor unset while PD elimination talk circulates).

**Consequences:** Whatever the memo proposes becomes the anchor. Risk accepted: if a department-wide standard emerges, this reads as pre-negotiation — mitigated by decision 0001's clarification framing. Items dropped from the memo so far: Spirit Squad (continuing work, fully understood), AP Clinic (Courteney Tompkins owns it; Eric assists at her direction).

---

## 0003 — Linda in the memo as a question, not a proposal; Blake removed from all forward planning

**Status:** accepted 2026-07-17

**Context:** The JD names AJ (AP Specialist, football) and Noah (BB AP GA) but is silent on Linda and Blake. The Jul 9 meeting made "clarify Linda and Blake's positions" a joint Eric/Chris action item, and leadership stated Eric's role toward Linda is supportive, not directive. **Fact established this session: Blake has left the organization entirely.**

**Decision:** The memo's second clarification item names Linda's role definition as open and to be resolved in the upcoming Eric/Chris conversation — Eric asks, he does not propose her structure. Blake is removed from the OKR unit and all forward planning; his KR co-ownership redistributes across Eric and AJ.

**Alternatives considered:** Proposing Linda's structure in the memo (crosses the supportive-not-directive boundary Chris drew); leaving Linda out entirely (ignores a named action item).

**Consequences:** Q1-remainder staffing math is Eric + AJ + Noah (GA). Capacity case for de-scoping at least one output KR (white paper) strengthens. OKR doc's unit_members and KR ownership lines must be rewritten.

---

## 0004 — Fall-camp framework and Aranda review hand off fully to AJ

**Status:** accepted 2026-07-17

**Context:** The JD grants AJ "big picture planning and communications w/FB Staff." Current KR 1.2 has Eric delivering the FaceComps color-coded load framework for 100% of fall-camp practices and presenting the plan-vs-actual review to Aranda — Eric's single most visible coaching-staff touchpoint. The framework has already been presented to staff in a shared meeting; AJ has run day-to-day for a while and is ready.

**Decision:** Full handoff now. AJ owns camp planning and presents to Aranda; Eric reviews artifacts pre-delivery, co-builds the analysis, and owns the standards/templates ([[CONTEXT]] → Oversee).

**Alternatives considered:** Shared presentation through camp (transition already effectively complete — adds nothing); Eric retains through camp (contradicts the JD he is about to accept, in the highest-pressure month).

**Consequences:** Eric's visibility channel for this work moves from the Aranda room to the biweekly report to Chris, where the story becomes proof the director model works. KR 1.2 is rewritten with AJ as owner, Eric as reviewer.

---

## 0005 — White paper stays at drafted-by-Aug-31, Eric sole owner, zero dependency on Blake

**Status:** accepted 2026-07-17

**Context:** Blake (departed) was co-authoring the white paper and left behind a short report that converts readily into a draft. Blake may still contribute material voluntarily, but he is outside the organization with no obligation or deadline Eric controls.

**Decision:** KR 3.3 keeps its Aug 31 drafted target. Eric solely owns the critical path — converting the existing short report into the white paper draft. Blake is credited as co-author for work done; any post-departure contribution is bonus, never a dependency. Publication deployment remains Q2 as originally planned.

**Alternatives considered:** De-scope to "scoped" (undersells — draft material already exists); defer to Q2 with Blake on the critical path (bets the August review on a departed collaborator's follow-through).

**Consequences:** R&D pillar keeps its output KR alongside the new BAIR infrastructure KRs. If conversion proves bigger than expected, the fallback is an honest re-date at the August review, not a quiet miss.

---

## 0006 — Education engine reset: 2 module-anchored issues, launch decoupled from website and from approval

**Status:** accepted 2026-07-17

**Context:** Original KR 2.1 (twice monthly, 6 issues by Aug 31) is 0-for-3 at mid-July. Template and content ideas exist; the real blockers are an open-ended comfort/sign-off loop and distribution being re-planned around a not-yet-launched website (Cody). The Jul 9 meeting explicitly directed: circulate drafts, don't wait for permission.

**Decision:** KR 2.1 resets to 2 issues by Aug 31 — Issue #1 by ~Aug 1 anchored by the sleep education module, Issue #2 by ~Aug 22 anchored by the GLP-1 brief, both modules circulated to named stakeholders. The proof-of-concept goes out advance-notice style ("distributing Aug 1 unless changes requested"), and launch ships by email to existing lists; the website is the Q2 distribution upgrade, not a Q1 gate.

**Alternatives considered:** Hold at 6 (already unachievable — re-signs the quiet-miss pattern); push 3 issues (no pre-written material waiting, unlike the white paper).

**Consequences:** August review sets ongoing cadence from evidence. The launched-at-modest-cadence story replaces the behind-on-six story. Ship date of Issue #1 is the KR's teeth.

---

## 0007 — Semester OKR cycles with mandatory mid-semester checkpoints

**Status:** accepted 2026-07-17

**Context:** Eric proposed replacing quarterly OKR cycles with semester-long ones (Aug–Dec, Jan–May) to match the athletic calendar and the true duration of infrastructure builds. Risk named and accepted: his self-identified failure mode is execution in accountability-free environments, and the newsletter went 0-for-6 with a quarterly clock running; the Jul 9 meeting asked for more visibility, not less.

**Decision:** Semester-scoped objectives and KRs — the current summer block closes out at the already-promised Aug 31 review; Fall runs Sep 1–Dec 31, Spring Jan–May — with a non-negotiable mid-semester checkpoint (~Oct 15, ~Mar 1) formally scoring every KR on-track/off-track, and the biweekly Chris report as the standing pulse. KR horizons double; inspection frequency does not.

**Alternatives considered:** Pure semesters with no midpoint (maximizes the drift risk); keeping quarters with bigger KRs (retains re-authoring overhead and misfits the calendar).

**Consequences:** The memo announces the structure as designed system, not stretched deadline. Also resolved this turn: tech decision matrix is the completed Q1 flagship (applied to the live Firstbeat 10-license decision), HPI protocol v1 is the drafted item (agenda for the proactive Kenny meeting), continuity plan stages to Fall. Infrastructure flagship logic: smallest first, visible fast.

---

## 0008 — "Unified dashboard" rewritten: standardize the data layer, deliver bespoke per sport

**Status:** accepted 2026-07-17

**Context:** KR 1.1 committed to a single unified coach-facing dashboard (Football + Volleyball). Eric's operating reality: a single dashboard across programs isn't right and likely never will be — sport delivery is bespoke one-off dashboards and reports, and staying plugged into that bespoke creation is one of his hands-on lanes.

**Decision:** KR 1.1 becomes: per-sport coach-facing dashboards in routine weekly use (Football delivered through AJ, Volleyball direct), built on shared data standards — common metric definitions, data model, and freshness expectations — with bespoke presentation per sport. Adoption teeth unchanged (referenced in the team's weekly planning meeting ≥5 of 6 weeks). Glossary: "unified" = standardized underneath, bespoke on top ([[CONTEXT]]).

**Alternatives considered:** Keeping the single-dashboard aspiration — commits to a UI consolidation nobody asked for and a "not adopted" report in December for a thing Eric doesn't believe in.

**Consequences:** Eric's personal lanes (HPI protocol + dashboarding, tech vetting, white-paper analysis, one-off report/dashboard creation) and the delegated sport delivery reinforce rather than compete: the HPI protocol and continuity plan are the standardization instrument the per-sport dashboards sit on.

---

## 0009 — Tech matrix KR: adoption is the bar, no named vendor

**Status:** accepted 2026-07-17 (amends 0007's Firstbeat reference)

**Context:** The matrix KR was first drafted as "applied to the live Firstbeat decision." Eric pulled Firstbeat out; the counter-proposal "matrix exists" was rejected because existence is the bar that already failed — the Jul 9 meeting's problem statement was reviving *unused* frameworks, and a document nobody is bound to is shelf-ware regardless of date.

**Decision:** KR 1.2 = matrix revived and **adopted as standard vendor intake** — documented + Chris sign-off in writing, advance-notice style. No vendor named in the KR; forcing it onto a product nobody wants is theater. The next real pitch simply flows through the process.

**Alternatives considered:** Anchor to a named live decision (makes the KR hostage to an external party's negotiation pace — the exact failure property the newsletter taught); existence-only (repeats the original shelf-ware outcome).

**Consequences:** Establishes the v3 design rule now written into the OKR doc: every KR's critical path stays inside the unit's control. Firstbeat follow-up remains an inbox item on its own merits, decoupled from the OKR set.

---

## 0010 — Department briefing is a reusable asset; v1 deployment targets admins + sport admins

**Status:** accepted 2026-07-18

**Context:** Recent conversations surfaced that administrative stakeholders don't have a clear picture of what Applied Performance does. Grilling the briefing plan revealed four candidate audiences (administrators, sport program admins, head coaches, support staff via H&W onboarding) — one fixed deck cannot serve them all, and building for everyone fails the retell test.

**Decision:** Build a **Briefing Asset** ([[CONTEXT]]) — three pillars + capability menu + one-sentence mission — deployed per room. V1 deployment is the admin/sport-admin briefing, delivered as a slot in an existing admin meeting. The slot request is triggered by deck v1 existing (with a self-imposed deck deadline to prevent drift), not by a calendar date picked first. Head-coach variant and H&W-onboarding module are staged derivatives.

**Alternatives considered:** One general-audience talk (generality kills the ask and the retell test); onboarding module first (slower path to the room that prompted this); requesting the slot before content exists (commits before proof points exist — though the standing biweekly email can still seed the three-pillar language).

**Consequences:** Deck v1 must be modular enough to re-wrap. The plan doc (SecondBrain\Projects\Applied-Performance-Stakeholder-Briefing-Plan.md) is amended by this session's outcomes. Derivative deployments are Fall candidates, not current scope.

---

## Session close — artifacts drafted 2026-07-17

Memo: [[JD-feedback-memo-2026-07-20]]. OKR v3: [[Applied-Performance-OKRs-2026-27]] (superseded list at bottom maps v2 → v3 against these records). Operating mechanics settled without ADR: Friday biweekly email to Chris (his stated preference), five fixed headings, <300 words; decision-impact log demoted to report fuel.

corpus, but no document lists them as served groups. Real work is happening in lanes
none of your planning documents describe, which is its own kind of invisibility.

volleyball, that involvement is currently invisible in every system you have — which

14	**Why this exists.** "I would start one project, work a little on it, and start a new one because of a random idea or a suggestion. Nothing had a deadline. Done was never defined." — 2026-09-14. Four earlier fixes died because each had to be remembered. These rules are checked by a timer, not by memory.
15	
16	## The four rules
17	
18	**1. Active only with a charter.** A job project is active only when it has:
19	- **Pillar** — data, education, or research — and the JD duty it serves.
20	- **Receiver** — a named person who asked for it or agreed to receive it. *No name, not active.*
21	- **Done means** — one sentence: the thing handed over.
22	- **4 dated steps** — Plan agreed with receiver → First draft to receiver → Final delivered → Receiver confirms it is in use.
23	- **Finish date** — on or before semester close (2026-12-18).
24	
25	**2. Four active, no more.** A new project starts only when one is finished or dropped. The one waiting for a slot is "next up." *Fall 2026 exception: cap is 5 so research keeps one project (decided 2026-09-14). Back to 4 in Spring 2027.*
26	
27	**3. Ideas wait.** New ideas and suggestions go to `/project idea`. Flag an idea only if it has a pillar **and** a receiver. It still waits for a slot.
28	
29	**4. The timer checks.** `KeystoneOS/scripts/ritual-check.ps1` runs `portfolio.py slate-check` and raises a desktop prompt when:
30	- more than 4 job projects are active,
31	- a step date passed and the step is not done,
32	- a project is past its finish date,
33	- the Oct 15 checkpoint or Dec 18 semester close was missed,
34	- an active project has no full charter,
35	- a slot is open and a project is waiting.

40	|---|---|

# BAIR — transferred project context

Carried over from the Claude cloud project, Sept 2026.

## Mission and positioning

BAIR evaluates, approves, and supports research proposals aligned with three strategic
pillars: Human Performance, Character Formation, and Business Enterprise. Baylor's
position as a Christian R1 institution with Power 4 athletics is a deliberate part of
BAIR's identity and strategic framing, not incidental.

BAIR coordinates across Health & Wellness: Athletic Medicine, Mental Health & Wellness,
Sports Nutrition, and Strength & Conditioning.

## People

| Person | Role | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Kenny Boyd | Executive Senior Associate AD | Eric reports to him; prefers quick visual scanning over dense docs |
| Dr. Andrew Gallucci | Research team lead | Central to framework development and proposal review |
| Blake Wright | Applied Performance PhD Fellow | Bilateral asymmetries project |
| Jeremy Frazier | Staff physical therapist | PI on fitness predictors / injury outcomes |
| Dr. Sarah Snitker | Robbins College | Collaborator |
| Doug McNamee | Senior leadership | Visibility target |

Campus partners: Truett Seminary, the Bright Center, Robbins College.

## Evaluation framework

Five scored dimensions:

| Dimension | Weight |
|---|---|
| Strategic Alignment | 31% |
| Athlete & Staff Burden | 26% |
| Revenue & Resources | 20% |
| Research Quality | 15% |
| Gender Equity | 10% |

Feasibility is a binary gatekeeper, not a scored dimension. Review is dual-track with a
conservative default to full committee review.

## What has proven true in review

- **Athlete burden is the top practical constraint.** High athlete time triggers full
  committee review automatically and carries a heavy scoring penalty. Collapsing
  multi-phase designs or piggybacking on existing sessions dramatically improves viability.
- **Internal PI positioning matters.** Proposals that read as extractive external research
  score poorly. Repositioning with an internal PI plus internal resources changes the
  strategic calculus substantially.
- **"Start strict, loosen later."** Gallucci's principle: you can't undo a yes. This is
  why the review defaults are conservative.
- **Gender equity is an incentive, not an exclusion.** The framework rewards inclusive
  designs rather than penalizing single-gender studies.
- **Plain language beats institutional prose.** Formal, promotional, or bureaucratic
  writing actively undermines credibility with this audience.

## Active pipeline

- **Blake Wright** — bilateral asymmetries and lower-extremity injury. Approved at
  moderate priority; data transfer underway via encrypted, deidentified transfer.
- **Jeremy Frazier** — prospective cohort on fitness predictors and injury outcomes.
  Single-phase design, ~30-minute baseline during pre-season, 14-month timeline, zero
  budget on existing infrastructure.
- DXA/injury analysis and published women's soccer body composition work also in portfolio.

## On the horizon

Campus collaboration development with Truett Seminary, Robbins College, and the Bright
Center. The Educational Alignment Initiative proposes BAIR as cross-departmental
custodian of athlete-facing education. Continued pipeline development, committee review
cycles, and expanding visibility with senior leadership.

## Ways of working

- Oversight runs by email, not meetings. Routine check-ins (Blake's progress) are monthly email.
- MS Teams is BAIR's virtual home. MS Planner for visual project tracking, Excel for
  detailed metrics, built for leadership-friendly visual scanning.
- Formatting is calibrated to audience: dense reference docs for the committee,
  scannable dashboards for leadership.
- Expect multiple revision passes with specific targeted feedback.
- Fireflies retrieves meeting transcripts before drafting follow-ups. Search pattern:
  keyword plus date filter, then fetch by transcript ID.
- Parse uploaded .docx via dedicated extraction, not raw read tools.
- html2pptx / pptxgen for PowerPoint: slide dimensions 960x540px, watch font sizing.

# Baylor Sport Science — internship curriculum

The **content** of the Applied Performance internship program: what an intern reads,
what they do, and how they are assessed. Split out of `AgentAssist` on 2026-08-18.

```
modules.md    eleven modules in four blocks — the sequence an intern works through
handbook.md   the intern-facing handbook, written in second person
cpss-text/    the NSCA CPSS source material and the structural notes taken from it
              (PDFs and PPTXs are gitignored — purchased material, never pushed)
```

## The split, and why

`AgentAssist` is the **machine** — the question ledger, the agents, the deterministic
tools, the competency taxonomy, the education log. This repo is the **content** those
agents plan against. Keeping them apart means curriculum edits do not churn the plugin,
and plugin edits do not churn the curriculum.

The line:

| Lives here | Lives in `AgentAssist` |
|---|---|
| Module list, readings, tasks, evidence | `context/competencies.md` — the eight domain codes |
| Intern handbook | `context/department.md` — department facts |
| CPSS source material and chapter map | `context/measurement-standards.md` — the analytical spine |
| | `docs/education-log.md` — sessions actually delivered |
| | `agents/curriculum-architect.md` — the agent that edits this repo |

Paths written as `AgentAssist/...` in these files point at the sibling repo at
`~/DEV/AgentAssist`.

## The one design decision to preserve

**A module is not a PowerPoint Eric builds.** Applied Performance is one person with no
protected time. The staff deck series produced three decks and stopped; eleven intern
decks would stop faster. So the intern does the reading and the task, and the twenty
minutes of discussion is the only cost to Eric.

Slides accumulate rather than being built up front. When the same explanation has come
up in discussion three or four times, *then* it is worth a deck — and by then it writes
itself. See `modules.md` for the full statement of this.

## Status

Draft v1, 2026-08-18. Reading assignments are filled from the real CPSS chapter list
(31 chapters across 7 Parts). **Chapter assignments are proposed, not signed off** —
Eric picks the final set.

## Not CPSS exam preparation

Deliberate scope choice, not a gap. The text is a content spine and a standing
reference. Nobody here is optimising for someone sitting the exam.

# BAIR — transferred project context

Carried over from the Claude cloud project, Sept 2026.

## Mission and positioning

BAIR evaluates, approves, and supports research proposals aligned with three strategic
pillars: Human Performance, Character Formation, and Business Enterprise. Baylor's
position as a Christian R1 institution with Power 4 athletics is a deliberate part of
BAIR's identity and strategic framing, not incidental.

BAIR coordinates across Health & Wellness: Athletic Medicine, Mental Health & Wellness,
Sports Nutrition, and Strength & Conditioning.

## People

| Person | Role | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Kenny Boyd | Executive Senior Associate AD | Eric reports to him; prefers quick visual scanning over dense docs |
| Dr. Andrew Gallucci | Research team lead | Central to framework development and proposal review |
| Blake Wright | Applied Performance PhD Fellow | Bilateral asymmetries project |
| Jeremy Frazier | Staff physical therapist | PI on fitness predictors / injury outcomes |
| Dr. Sarah Snitker | Robbins College | Collaborator |
| Doug McNamee | Senior leadership | Visibility target |

Campus partners: Truett Seminary, the Bright Center, Robbins College.

## Evaluation framework

Five scored dimensions:

| Dimension | Weight |
|---|---|
| Strategic Alignment | 31% |
| Athlete & Staff Burden | 26% |
| Revenue & Resources | 20% |
| Research Quality | 15% |
| Gender Equity | 10% |

Feasibility is a binary gatekeeper, not a scored dimension. Review is dual-track with a
conservative default to full committee review.

## What has proven true in review

- **Athlete burden is the top practical constraint.** High athlete time triggers full
  committee review automatically and carries a heavy scoring penalty. Collapsing
  multi-phase designs or piggybacking on existing sessions dramatically improves viability.
- **Internal PI positioning matters.** Proposals that read as extractive external research
  score poorly. Repositioning with an internal PI plus internal resources changes the
  strategic calculus substantially.
- **"Start strict, loosen later."** Gallucci's principle: you can't undo a yes. This is
  why the review defaults are conservative.
- **Gender equity is an incentive, not an exclusion.** The framework rewards inclusive
  designs rather than penalizing single-gender studies.
- **Plain language beats institutional prose.** Formal, promotional, or bureaucratic
  writing actively undermines credibility with this audience.

## Active pipeline

- **Blake Wright** — bilateral asymmetries and lower-extremity injury. Approved at
  moderate priority; data transfer underway via encrypted, deidentified transfer.
- **Jeremy Frazier** — prospective cohort on fitness predictors and injury outcomes.
  Single-phase design, ~30-minute baseline during pre-season, 14-month timeline, zero
  budget on existing infrastructure.
- DXA/injury analysis and published women's soccer body composition work also in portfolio.

## On the horizon

Campus collaboration development with Truett Seminary, Robbins College, and the Bright
Center. The Educational Alignment Initiative proposes BAIR as cross-departmental
custodian of athlete-facing education. Continued pipeline development, committee review
cycles, and expanding visibility with senior leadership.

## Ways of working

- Oversight runs by email, not meetings. Routine check-ins (Blake's progress) are monthly email.
- MS Teams is BAIR's virtual home. MS Planner for visual project tracking, Excel for
  detailed metrics, built for leadership-friendly visual scanning.
- Formatting is calibrated to audience: dense reference docs for the committee,
  scannable dashboards for leadership.
- Expect multiple revision passes with specific targeted feedback.
- Fireflies retrieves meeting transcripts before drafting follow-ups. Search pattern:
  keyword plus date filter, then fetch by transcript ID.
- Parse uploaded .docx via dedicated extraction, not raw read tools.
- html2pptx / pptxgen for PowerPoint: slide dimensions 960x540px, watch font sizing.

# Baylor Sport Science — internship curriculum

The **content** of the Applied Performance internship program: what an intern reads,
what they do, and how they are assessed. Split out of `AgentAssist` on 2026-08-18.

```
modules.md    eleven modules in four blocks — the sequence an intern works through
handbook.md   the intern-facing handbook, written in second person
cpss-text/    the NSCA CPSS source material and the structural notes taken from it
              (PDFs and PPTXs are gitignored — purchased material, never pushed)
```

## The split, and why

`AgentAssist` is the **machine** — the question ledger, the agents, the deterministic
tools, the competency taxonomy, the education log. This repo is the **content** those
agents plan against. Keeping them apart means curriculum edits do not churn the plugin,
and plugin edits do not churn the curriculum.

The line:

| Lives here | Lives in `AgentAssist` |
|---|---|
| Module list, readings, tasks, evidence | `context/competencies.md` — the eight domain codes |
| Intern handbook | `context/department.md` — department facts |
| CPSS source material and chapter map | `context/measurement-standards.md` — the analytical spine |
| | `docs/education-log.md` — sessions actually delivered |
| | `agents/curriculum-architect.md` — the agent that edits this repo |

Paths written as `AgentAssist/...` in these files point at the sibling repo at
`~/DEV/AgentAssist`.

## The one design decision to preserve

**A module is not a PowerPoint Eric builds.** Applied Performance is one person with no
protected time. The staff deck series produced three decks and stopped; eleven intern
decks would stop faster. So the intern does the reading and the task, and the twenty
minutes of discussion is the only cost to Eric.

Slides accumulate rather than being built up front. When the same explanation has come
up in discussion three or four times, *then* it is worth a deck — and by then it writes
itself. See `modules.md` for the full statement of this.

## Status

Draft v1, 2026-08-18. Reading assignments are filled from the real CPSS chapter list
(31 chapters across 7 Parts). **Chapter assignments are proposed, not signed off** —
Eric picks the final set.

## Not CPSS exam preparation

Deliberate scope choice, not a gap. The text is a content spine and a standing
reference. Nobody here is optimising for someone sitting the exam.
